main_replacements.anchor_exact: We obtained the initial prompt box from the tight bounding box of the nonempty reference mask, expanded each horizontal side by 10 % of the width and each vertical side by 10 % of the height, and clipped the result to the image. This is a reference-informed, known-location (oracle-localization) setting, not a test of autonomous lesion localization. We encoded the image once and used the resulting embedding for the initial prediction and four additional predictions (Figure 2). The fixed 10 % context margin was used consistently across datasets.

blocks.text: We obtained the initial prompt box from the tight bounding box of the nonempty reference mask, using half-open pixel bounds with upper coordinates one pixel beyond the last foreground index, expanded each horizontal side by 10 % of the width and each vertical side by 10 % of the height, and clipped the result to the image. This is a reference-informed, known-location (oracle-localization) setting, not a test of autonomous lesion localization. We encoded the image once and used the resulting embedding for the initial prediction and four additional predictions (Figure 2). The fixed 10 % context margin was used consistently across datasets.

main_replacements.anchor_exact: Method A calculated risk as one minus the raw predicted intersection over union (IoU) returned for the initial mask. For method B, we shifted the initial clipped box left and right by 5 % of its width and up and down by 5 % of its height, clipping each shifted box to the image. We calculated the Dice coefficient between the initial predicted mask and each of the four shifted-prompt masks. Risk B was one minus the mean of these four Dice coefficients. We retained all four directions when clipping produced coincident boxes. The consistency Dice coefficient was defined as 1 when both predicted masks were empty. The 5 % translations define a deterministic local stability probe relative to box size. Method B adds four mask-decoder passes while reusing the image embedding. Recorded inference times cover the combined pipeline; A-only and incremental B times were not separately benchmarked.

main_replacements.anchor_exact: For binary masks, the Dice coefficient is twice the number of shared foreground pixels divided by the sum of foreground pixels in the two masks. The quality reference for both methods was Dice between the initial prediction and the manual mask. An empty initial prediction against a nonempty reference would contribute a Dice coefficient of 0. We defined low quality as reference Dice below 0.70, an operational cutoff for this evaluation.

blocks.text: The quality reference for both methods was the initial prediction’s Dice against the manual mask, $D(P_0,G)$ in Eq. (1). An empty initial prediction against the nonempty reference has Dice zero. Low quality was defined as reference Dice below 0.70, an operational cutoff for this evaluation. The raw model confidence in Eq. (2) and prediction-consistency score in Eq. (3) remain separate from this reference-quality outcome.

main_replacements.anchor_exact: The analysis included cases with a valid reference Dice and both finite risk scores. The procedure allowed one retry with the same configuration after a technical failure and recorded persistent failures separately. We report low-quality detection as the number of flagged low-quality masks divided by the number of low-quality masks. Simulated review is the number of flagged cases divided by all scored cases. Misses per 100 patients is 100 times the number of unflagged low-quality masks divided by all scored cases.

main_replacements.anchor_exact: As post hoc descriptive quality-control measures, we additionally tabulated true-positive (TP), false-positive (FP), true-negative (TN) and false-negative (FN) counts, sensitivity (TP/(TP+FN)), specificity (TN/(TN+FP)), positive predictive value (PPV; TP/(TP+FP)) and negative predictive value (NPV; TN/(TN+FN)). Low-quality segmentation was the positive condition and a review flag the positive test. We used Wilson 95 % intervals for these proportions. These measures assess mask-quality screening, not diagnosis of breast cancer.

blocks.text: As post hoc descriptive quality-control measures, we additionally tabulated true-positive (TP), false-positive (FP), true-negative (TN) and false-negative (FN) counts, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV), with Wilson 95 % intervals (Tables S6 and S7). Low-quality segmentation was the positive condition and a review flag the positive test. These measures assess mask-quality screening, not diagnosis of breast cancer.

main_replacements.anchor_exact: We also used symmetric Kitagawa accounting and direct standardization across dataset-reported benign/malignant strata [13]. The external-minus-internal difference was partitioned into a composition-associated term and a within-stratum-rate term. Common weights were the arithmetic mean of the two cohort weights. Detection used the diagnostic shares among low-quality masks, whereas review fractions used shares among all scored patients. We obtained nominal percentile intervals from 5,000 independently sampled cohort-level patient-bootstrap replicates (seed 20261107), recalculating all weights and rates. Undefined stratum denominators remained missing. This accounting describes the observed mixtures and does not estimate causal effects.

supplement_replacements.anchor_exact: Symmetric Kitagawa identity: overall difference = Σ[(wE−wI)(pE+pI)/2] + Σ[(pE−pI)(wE+wI)/2]. Detection weights are the diagnostic proportions among low-quality cases; review weights are the diagnostic proportions among all patients. The first sum is composition-associated and the second is the within-stratum term. Weights are recomputed in every draw.

blocks.text: For diagnostic stratum $s$, let $w_{c,s}$ be its weight and $p_{c,s}$ its outcome rate in cohort $c$, with E denoting external and I internal testing. For detection, weights are diagnostic shares among low-quality patients and rates are stratum-specific low-quality detection. For review, weights are diagnostic shares among all scored patients and rates are stratum-specific review fractions. Rates in Eqs. (S1) and (S2) are fractions; Table S12 reports differences in percentage points. The symmetric Kitagawa composition-associated term and within-stratum-rate term are
Together, $C$ and $W$ sum to the external-minus-internal overall rate difference when the stratum rates are defined. Weights and rates are recomputed in each bootstrap draw.

supplement_replacements.anchor_exact: For diagnostic stratum s, C = Σ(w_E,s−w_I,s)(p_E,s+p_I,s)/2 and W = Σ(p_E,s−p_I,s)(w_E,s+w_I,s)/2, so D=C+W. Common weights w*=(w_E+w_I)/2 give a standardized external-minus-internal difference equal to W. Components may not sum to the displayed total after rounding. Method: Kitagawa EM, J Am Stat Assoc 1955;50:1168–1194, doi:10.1080/01621459.1955.10501299.

blocks.text: Direct standardization uses the arithmetic mean of the two cohort weights for each diagnostic stratum. When the stratum rates are defined, the resulting standardized external-minus-internal difference equals the within-stratum-rate term $W$ in Eq. (S2). Overall rates are calculated directly from aggregate numerators and denominators. Components may not sum to the displayed total after rounding. Method: Kitagawa EM, J Am Stat Assoc 1955;50:1168–1194, doi:10.1080/01621459.1955.10501299.

formula_selection_rationale: Dice supplies the common quality/agreement definition. The two risks define the methods being compared. The two Kitagawa terms are the only unfamiliar mathematical accounting operation retained in the exploratory supplement.
